analysis.one_liner: Lets app-based gig platforms classify their workers as independent contractors outside wage, leave, and union laws
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written gig-worker status into federal law: anyone matching four criteria common to apps like Uber (setting their own hours, being rated by customers, getting electronic receipts, using their own equipment) would be an independent contractor, not an employee. That would take them outside the federal minimum wage and overtime law, unpaid family and medical leave, and the right to unionize. The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to two subcommittees, but no action ever followed.
analysis.who_benefits: App-based platform companies. Locking in independent-contractor status would spare them minimum wage, overtime, payroll taxes, leave obligations, and misclassification lawsuits, and would keep their workers from organizing under federal labor law.

how_it_helps.text: It exempts gig workers from the Fair Labor Standards Act, which guarantees a federal minimum wage and overtime pay after 40 hours a week.
It also exempts them from the Family and Medical Leave Act, which entitles eligible employees to unpaid, job-protected leave for serious illness or a new child.
It exempts them from the National Labor Relations Act, so they could not unionize or bargain collectively under federal law.

The four qualifying conditions — worker sets own hours, is rated by customers, gets electronic receipts, uses own tools — track the standard ride-hailing and delivery app business model, so the bill would shield that model directly.

analysis.who_pays: Gig workers themselves. They would keep bearing their own vehicle, fuel, and insurance costs with no wage floor, no overtime, no protected leave, and no federal right to organize.

drawbacks.text: Workers classified under the bill would have no federal minimum wage or overtime guarantee; after vehicle expenses, some ride-hailing drivers earn below minimum wage.
They would lose job-protected family and medical leave and the federal right to unionize, moving gig work permanently outside standard employment protections.
The bill would override ongoing misclassification disputes in the platforms' favor by statute, before courts could rule on whether these workers are employees under existing law.

The good-faith case for it: many gig workers say they value choosing their own hours, and applying employee rules rigidly could force platforms to schedule them like employees and erode that flexibility. The bill's four criteria were written to preserve that arrangement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow almost entirely to platform companies, which would shed wage, leave, and organizing obligations and the legal risk of misclassification suits. The costs fall on workers, who would keep all the business expenses and uncertainty while losing the core federal protections employees rely on. For working people, the bill was a net loss; the strongest argument for it — preserving scheduling flexibility — protects a business arrangement rather than a wage or benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to two subcommittees, but the committee never scheduled a hearing or vote, and it expired when the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David Schweikert introduced the bill on July 18, 2016, with no cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the day it was introduced.
On September 19, 2016, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections and the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was taken, and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gig workers, who kept at least the existing legal openings for minimum wage, leave, and organizing claims that the bill would have closed. Platform companies avoided neither a gain nor a loss; the issue simply stayed unresolved.

for.name: Rep. David Schweikert
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt qualifying gig workers from federal wage, leave, and labor laws.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled a markup, hearing, or vote on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote; the bill's only support was its single Republican sponsor, and no other member of either party signed on.

industries.note: The bill would have locked in independent-contractor status for the workers these platforms match through their apps, freeing the companies from minimum wage, overtime, leave, and collective-bargaining obligations and from misclassification lawsuits. The gain to the companies is a direct cost to the workers doing the jobs. The bill died before taking effect, so platforms gained nothing from it in law.

By excluding gig workers from the National Labor Relations Act, the bill would have barred them from federal union rights, shrinking the pool of workers unions could organize. It never advanced, so organizing pathways remained open.
